subject: Career
title: Panel Interviews: Reading the Room
description: A quick, practical guide to Panel Interviews: Reading the Room.

hook.text: Five interviewers sit across from you. Each has different priorities. Who do you focus on?

buildup.text: In panel interviews, there's usually one decision-maker, one skeptic, and several observers.

discovery.text: Answer to the person who asked, but make eye contact with the whole panel. Include everyone.

twist.text: The quiet person might be the actual decision-maker. Never ignore the silent observer.

climax.text: Using each panelist's name when responding shows presence and respect.

punchline.text: In a panel, win the room — not just the questioner.

quiz.question: Who should you focus on in a panel interview?
options: The whole panel, including quiet members
Only the person who asked the question

details.summary: Panel interviews involve multiple interviewers with different roles, priorities, and evaluation criteria. Success requires reading each panelist's engagement and distributing attention strategically across all decision-makers.
details.whyItMatters: Focusing on the friendliest panelist while ignoring a skeptic is a common mistake. Every panelist typically has veto power, so winning the room means winning each individual.
takeaways: Make eye contact with the person who asked the question, then scan others
Identify each panelist's likely priority based on their role
Address the skeptic directly rather than avoiding their gaze

faq.question: How do you prepare differently for a panel interview versus a one-on-one?
faq.answer: Research each panelist and prepare answers that address different functional priorities. Practice distributing eye contact and shortening answers slightly, since panel interviews often have tighter time constraints with more questions.

faq.question: What should you do if panel members seem to disagree with each other during your interview?
faq.answer: Stay neutral and avoid siding with either party. Acknowledge both perspectives diplomatically. Internal disagreements during your interview actually provide valuable insight into team dynamics and potential political landmines.
